lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Turn electron flow into ATP
lessons.subtitle: Complexes, carriers, proton pumping, inhibitors, and uncoupling

visual.caption: Electrons move downhill to oxygen while proton pumping stores the released energy as a gradient.

items.label: Entry
items.detail: NADH enters at Complex I; FADH2-derived electrons commonly enter at Complex II. Complex II does not pump protons.

items.label: Mobile carriers
items.detail: Coenzyme Q carries electrons within the membrane from I/II to III; cytochrome c carries them from III to IV.

items.label: Oxygen
items.detail: Complex IV transfers electrons to O2, forming water. Cyanide and CO block this terminal step.

items.label: ATP synthase
items.detail: Protons return to the matrix through F0F1 ATP synthase, driving phosphorylation of ADP.

items.label: Uncoupling
items.detail: A proton leak accelerates fuel oxidation and oxygen use but lowers ATP yield and releases energy as heat.
items.cue: More O2, less ATP, more heat

essentials: Complexes I, III, and IV pump protons; Complex II does not.
NADH yields about 2.5 ATP and FADH2 about 1.5 ATP because FADH2 bypasses Complex I.
Oligomycin blocks ATP synthase; rotenone blocks I, antimycin blocks III, and cyanide/CO block IV.
UCP1 in brown adipose tissue produces heat by permitting proton return without ATP formation.
Superoxide dismutase forms H2O2; catalase and selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidase remove peroxide.

traps.wrong: A negative delta G means a reaction must be fast.
traps.right: Delta G describes thermodynamic direction; activation energy and enzymes determine rate.

traps.wrong: Uncoupling stops electron transport.
traps.right: Uncoupling usually accelerates electron transport while decreasing ATP production.

recognition: No oxygen use after cyanide points to Complex IV blockade.
High oxygen consumption with heat and low ATP points to uncoupling.
Electron entry through Complex II produces less ATP because one proton-pumping site is bypassed.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Build collagen inside, finish it outside
lessons.subtitle: Triple helices, collagen types, cross-links, elastin, and classic diseases

visual.caption: Collagen synthesis crosses the ER, Golgi, extracellular cleavage, and cross-linking compartments.

items.label: Translate
items.detail: Prepro-alpha chains enter RER and lose signal peptides. Their repeating sequence is Gly-X-Y.

items.label: Modify
items.detail: Vitamin C-dependent hydroxylation and selected hydroxylysine glycosylation occur in the ER.

items.label: Triple helix
items.detail: Three chains form soluble procollagen with terminal propeptides that prevent intracellular fibrils.

items.label: Extracellular finish
items.detail: Propeptides are cleaved to tropocollagen; copper-dependent lysyl oxidase forms covalent cross-links.

items.label: Elastic fiber
items.detail: Tropoelastin is cross-linked on a fibrillin scaffold; alpha1-antitrypsin protects it from neutrophil elastase.

essentials: Type I is found in bone, skin, tendon, and scar; type II in cartilage; type III in reticular fibers; type IV in basement membranes.
Scurvy impairs hydroxylation, osteogenesis imperfecta commonly affects type I collagen, and many Ehlers-Danlos forms affect processing or structure.
Lysyl oxidase requires copper and acts extracellularly.
Fibrillin defects cause Marfan syndrome; elastase injury is amplified in alpha1-antitrypsin deficiency.
Denaturation of collagen's triple helix produces gelatin.

traps.wrong: Vitamin C cross-links collagen extracellularly.
traps.right: Vitamin C supports intracellular hydroxylation; copper-dependent lysyl oxidase creates extracellular cross-links.

traps.wrong: Type IV collagen forms ordinary fibrils in tendon.
traps.right: Type IV forms sheet-like basement-membrane networks.

recognition: Fractures plus blue sclerae indicate type I collagen disease.
Bleeding gums and poor wound healing indicate impaired vitamin C-dependent hydroxylation.
Early emphysema plus liver disease suggests alpha1-antitrypsin deficiency.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Separate GAG, proteoglycan, and glycoprotein
lessons.subtitle: Architecture, charge, targeting, and mucopolysaccharidoses

visual.caption: The length, branching, linkage, and charge of carbohydrate identify the glycoconjugate.

items.label: GAG
items.detail: Long unbranched repeating disaccharides; sulfate and carboxyl groups attract water and resist compression.

items.label: Hyaluronan
items.detail: Very large, unsulfated GAG made at the plasma membrane and not covalently linked to a core protein.

items.label: Proteoglycan
items.detail: Core protein with multiple long GAG chains; carbohydrate dominates mass and charge.

items.label: Glycoprotein
items.detail: Protein bearing shorter branched oligosaccharides, often for receptors, enzymes, antibodies, or recognition.

items.label: Degradation
items.detail: Lysosomal hydrolase defects cause stepwise substrate accumulation; mannose-6-phosphate directs enzymes to lysosomes.
items.cue: Match missing enzyme to stored GAG

essentials: N-linked carbohydrate attaches to asparagine; O-linked carbohydrate commonly attaches to serine or threonine.
Hyaluronan is unsulfated and not covalently linked to core protein.
Heparin is highly sulfated and potentiates antithrombin.
Hurler is autosomal recessive with corneal clouding; Hunter is X-linked and generally lacks clouding.
Failure of mannose-6-phosphate tagging causes I-cell disease.

traps.wrong: Proteoglycans and glycoproteins are interchangeable terms.
traps.right: Proteoglycans contain long GAG chains; glycoproteins contain shorter branched oligosaccharides.

traps.wrong: Every GAG contains uronic acid.
traps.right: Keratan sulfate contains galactose instead of uronic acid.

recognition: A hydrated compression-resistant ECM points to negatively charged GAGs.
Coarse features plus corneal clouding suggest Hurler rather than Hunter.
Secreted lysosomal enzymes with cellular inclusions suggest defective mannose-6-phosphate targeting.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Follow dietary fat from lumen to liver
lessons.subtitle: Bile, enzymes, micelles, chylomicrons, LPL, and remnants

visual.caption: Long-chain dietary fat takes a lumen-micelle-enterocyte-chylomicron route.

items.label: Emulsify
items.detail: Bile salts create small droplets and increase surface area for pancreatic enzymes.

items.label: Digest
items.detail: Pancreatic lipase plus colipase yields 2-monoacylglycerol and free fatty acids; other enzymes release cholesterol and lysophospholipid.

items.label: Micelle
items.detail: Mixed micelles deliver long-chain products and fat-soluble vitamins through the unstirred layer.

items.label: Package
items.detail: Enterocytes re-esterify lipids and use MTP plus ApoB-48 to assemble chylomicrons for lymph.

items.label: Unload and return
items.detail: HDL donates ApoC-II and ApoE; LPL unloads TAG and ApoE directs remnants to liver.

essentials: Short- and medium-chain fatty acids can enter portal blood directly on albumin.
ApoB-48 is structural for chylomicrons; ApoC-II activates LPL; ApoE mediates remnant uptake.
Bile obstruction or pancreatic insufficiency causes steatorrhea and fat-soluble-vitamin deficiency.
MTP deficiency prevents ApoB lipoprotein assembly in abetalipoproteinemia.
Orlistat inhibits gastric and pancreatic lipases.

traps.wrong: Intact chylomicrons are components of intestinal micelles.
traps.right: Micelles are luminal bile-salt structures; chylomicrons are assembled inside enterocytes.

traps.wrong: Bile salts enzymatically hydrolyze triacylglycerol.
traps.right: Bile salts emulsify; pancreatic lipase performs hydrolysis.

recognition: Fat-soluble-vitamin deficiency plus acanthocytes suggests abetalipoproteinemia.
Creamy plasma and pancreatitis point to LPL or ApoC-II failure.
ApoE is the clue for hepatic remnant clearance.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.topic: Fatty acids, TAG, and ketone bodies
lessons.title: Switch between making fat and burning fat
lessons.subtitle: ACC, malonyl-CoA, carnitine, beta oxidation, and ketogenesis

visual.caption: Malonyl-CoA is the gatekeeper that prevents synthesis and oxidation from running together.

items.label: Fed signal
items.detail: Insulin activates ACC; citrate supplies cytosolic acetyl-CoA; malonyl-CoA rises.

items.label: Synthesis
items.detail: Fatty-acid synthase uses malonyl units and NADPH from PPP/malic enzyme to make palmitate.

items.label: Gate
items.detail: Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I, preventing long-chain acyl entry into mitochondria.

items.label: Fasting burn
items.detail: Low insulin activates adipose lipolysis and lowers malonyl-CoA; carnitine transport enables beta oxidation.

items.label: Ketones
items.detail: Liver mitochondrial acetyl-CoA forms ketones. Liver lacks thiophorase, and red cells lack mitochondria, so neither uses them.

essentials: ACC is biotin dependent and rate limiting for synthesis; fatty-acid synthase releases palmitate.
Long-chain acyl entry uses CPT-I, translocase, and CPT-II.
One beta-oxidation cycle yields FADH2, NADH, acetyl-CoA, and a chain shortened by two carbons.
Odd-chain fatty acids yield succinyl-CoA through biotin- and B12-dependent steps.
MCAD deficiency causes fasting hypoketotic hypoglycemia and dicarboxylic aciduria.

traps.wrong: High malonyl-CoA accelerates beta oxidation.
traps.right: Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I and therefore blocks long-chain beta oxidation.

traps.wrong: Liver is the principal user of ketone bodies.
traps.right: Liver exports ketones because it lacks thiophorase.

recognition: Fasting hypoglycemia with low ketones suggests a fatty-acid-oxidation defect.
Dicarboxylic aciduria indicates compensatory omega oxidation.
High mitochondrial NADH shifts acetoacetate toward beta-hydroxybutyrate.

source.label: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 6th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 16, Fatty Acid, Ketone Body, and Triacylglycerol Metabolism.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Read phospholipids, sphingolipids, and eicosanoids as one map
lessons.subtitle: Membrane backbones, storage diseases, and opposing inflammatory mediators

visual.caption: First identify the backbone, then the head group, then the enzyme that builds or degrades it.

items.label: Glycerol lipids
items.detail: Phosphatidic acid branches toward TAG and glycerophospholipids; cardiolipin marks inner mitochondria and DPPC marks surfactant.

items.label: Sphingolipid core
items.detail: Sphingosine plus fatty acid forms ceramide; phosphocholine makes sphingomyelin and sugars make glycosphingolipids.

items.label: Storage diseases
items.detail: Hex A-Tay-Sachs; sphingomyelinase-Niemann-Pick; glucocerebrosidase-Gaucher; alpha-gal A-Fabry.

items.label: COX branch
items.detail: Cyclooxygenase makes prostaglandins, prostacyclin, and thromboxanes; aspirin irreversibly blocks it.

items.label: LOX branch
items.detail: 5-lipoxygenase makes leukotrienes: LTB4 recruits neutrophils; LTC4/D4/E4 constrict bronchi.

essentials: Phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid from the sn-2 position.
TXA2 promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction; PGI2 opposes both.
Cerebrosides contain one sugar; gangliosides contain oligosaccharide plus sialic acid.
Tay-Sachs lacks hepatosplenomegaly; Niemann-Pick commonly has it.
Aspirin's platelet effect lasts because platelets cannot synthesize new COX.

traps.wrong: All cherry-red-macula diseases are the same.
traps.right: Organomegaly and the stored lipid/enzyme distinguish Tay-Sachs from Niemann-Pick.

traps.wrong: LTB4 is the main cysteinyl bronchoconstrictor.
traps.right: LTB4 is chemotactic; LTC4, LTD4, and LTE4 strongly bronchoconstrict.

recognition: Crumpled-paper macrophages identify Gaucher disease.
Angiokeratomas and acroparesthesias in an X-linked pattern identify Fabry disease.
Arachidonic-acid questions split immediately into COX versus LOX products.

source.label: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 6th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 17, Phospholipid, Glycosphingolipid, and Eicosanoid Metabolism.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Route every lipoprotein by origin, cargo, and apoprotein
lessons.subtitle: Cholesterol synthesis, reverse transport, familial disorders, and steroid entry

visual.caption: Origin and cargo identify the particle; apoproteins identify its next interaction.

items.label: Chylomicron
items.detail: Intestinal ApoB-48 particle carries dietary TAG; C-II activates LPL and E returns the remnant to liver.

items.label: VLDL to LDL
items.detail: Liver exports TAG in ApoB-100 VLDL; lipolysis creates IDL and cholesterol-rich LDL.

items.label: LDL
items.detail: ApoB-100 binds LDL receptor to deliver cholesterol; oxidized LDL enters macrophage scavenger receptors and forms foam cells.

items.label: HDL
items.detail: ApoA-I activates LCAT and supports reverse cholesterol transport; HDL also supplies C-II and E.

items.label: Cholesterol fate
items.detail: HMG-CoA reductase makes cholesterol; CYP7A1 begins bile-acid synthesis; StAR moves cholesterol into mitochondria for steroids.

essentials: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase and increase hepatic LDL-receptor expression.
LCAT esterifies cholesterol in plasma HDL; ACAT esterifies it inside cells.
ApoB-48 is chylomicron structural protein; ApoB-100 binds LDL receptor; ApoC-II activates LPL; ApoE clears remnants.
Familial hypercholesterolemia reduces LDL clearance; LPL/ApoC-II deficiency causes severe chylomicronemia.
Humans eliminate cholesterol through bile as free cholesterol or bile acids, not by complete oxidation.

traps.wrong: HDL mainly delivers dietary TAG.
traps.right: Chylomicrons deliver dietary TAG; HDL specializes in reverse cholesterol transport and apoprotein exchange.

traps.wrong: LCAT and ACAT act in the same compartment.
traps.right: LCAT acts in plasma on HDL; ACAT acts intracellularly.

recognition: Tendon xanthomas with very high LDL indicate defective LDL-receptor pathway.
Orange tonsils with very low HDL indicate ABCA1/Tangier disease.
Pancreatitis with creamy plasma indicates failure to clear chylomicron TAG.

source.label: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 6th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 18, Cholesterol, Lipoprotein, and Steroid Metabolism.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Let the insulin-to-glucagon ratio choose the pathway
lessons.subtitle: Secretion, receptors, tissue effects, and hypoglycemic patterns
topicPatterns: metabolic effects of insulin and glucagon

visual.caption: Insulin stores incoming fuel; glucagon preserves circulating fuel during fasting.

items.label: Beta-cell sensor
items.detail: Glucose raises ATP, closes KATP, depolarizes the cell, opens Ca2+ channels, and triggers insulin exocytosis.

items.label: Insulin signal
items.detail: Receptor tyrosine kinase signaling recruits GLUT4 in muscle/adipose and promotes glycogen, fat, and protein synthesis.

items.label: Glucagon signal
items.detail: Hepatic Gs-cAMP-PKA signaling promotes glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, fatty-acid oxidation, and ketogenesis.

items.label: C-peptide
items.detail: Endogenous insulin carries equimolar C-peptide; injected insulin does not.

items.label: Low glucose
items.detail: Autonomic symptoms warn first; neuroglycopenia causes confusion, seizures, and coma.

essentials: The insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase; the glucagon receptor is a Gs-coupled GPCR.
Liver uses GLUT2, not insulin-recruited GLUT4.
Skeletal muscle has little direct glucagon response.
An amino-acid meal can stimulate both insulin and glucagon.
High insulin plus high C-peptide suggests endogenous secretion; high insulin plus low C-peptide suggests injected insulin.

traps.wrong: Insulin opens beta-cell KATP channels.
traps.right: Glucose-derived ATP closes KATP channels, initiating depolarization.

traps.wrong: Ethanol provides extra gluconeogenic substrate.
traps.right: High NADH from ethanol diverts pyruvate and oxaloacetate away from gluconeogenesis.

recognition: Sulfonylureas close KATP and can cause hypoglycemia.
Tremor and sweating are autonomic; confusion and seizure are neuroglycopenic.
Endogenous hyperinsulinism is C-peptide positive.

source.label: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 6th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 23, Metabolic Effects of Insulin and Glucagon.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Track fuel by tissue across fed, overnight fast, and starvation
lessons.subtitle: Liver, adipose, muscle, brain, and red-cell priorities

visual.caption: As fasting lengthens, glycogen gives way to gluconeogenesis and then brain ketone use spares protein.

items.label: Fed
items.detail: High insulin drives hepatic glycogen/glycolysis/lipogenesis, adipose TAG storage, and muscle glycogen/protein synthesis.

items.label: Overnight fast
items.detail: Hepatic glycogenolysis dominates early while gluconeogenesis rises; adipose releases fatty acids and glycerol.

items.label: One day
items.detail: Liver glycogen wanes; lactate, alanine, and glycerol support gluconeogenesis using energy from beta oxidation.

items.label: Several days
items.detail: Liver makes ketones from fatty acids; brain increasingly uses them and reduces glucose demand.

items.label: Obligate glucose
items.detail: Red cells always require glucose and release lactate; some brain and renal-medullary needs also persist.

essentials: Even-chain fatty acids cannot provide net glucose; glycerol and odd-chain fatty acids can contribute.
Beta oxidation supplies ATP and acetyl-CoA to support gluconeogenesis.
Low malonyl-CoA opens CPT-I during fasting.
The Cori cycle carries lactate carbon; the alanine cycle also carries amino nitrogen.
Liver makes but cannot use ketones; red cells can neither make nor use them.

traps.wrong: The brain switches to long-chain fatty acids during starvation.
traps.right: The brain adapts to ketone bodies because long-chain fatty acids poorly cross the blood-brain barrier.

traps.wrong: Muscle glycogen directly maintains blood glucose.
traps.right: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and uses its glycogen locally.

recognition: Early fasting questions point to hepatic glycogen; prolonged fasting points to gluconeogenesis and ketones.
Falling urinary nitrogen after several days reflects brain ketone adaptation and protein sparing.
Albumin-bound fatty acids and glycerol both originate from adipose TAG lipolysis.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: See diabetes as uncontrolled fasting plus glucose toxicity
lessons.subtitle: Type 1 versus type 2, DKA versus HHS, diagnosis, and chronic injury

visual.caption: Insulin availability determines ketone risk; hyperglycemia and dehydration can be profound in both major types.

items.label: Type 1
items.detail: Autoimmune beta-cell destruction causes absolute insulin deficiency, low C-peptide, abrupt symptoms, and strong DKA risk.

items.label: Type 2
items.detail: Insulin resistance begins with compensatory insulin, then progressive beta-cell failure; obesity is a common driver.

items.label: DKA
items.detail: Low insulin permits HSL, fatty-acid delivery, ketogenesis, high-anion-gap acidosis, and total-body potassium loss.

items.label: HHS
items.detail: Residual insulin limits ketones, but extreme glucose causes osmotic diuresis, hyperosmolarity, and neurologic change.

items.label: Chronic damage
items.detail: AGEs, polyol flux, oxidative stress, and vascular injury drive retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, and atherosclerosis.

essentials: Diagnostic thresholds include fasting glucose at least 126 mg/dL and HbA1c at least 6.5% when appropriately confirmed.
HbA1c reflects roughly 2-3 months and can be misleading when red-cell lifespan is abnormal.
Hyperglycemia causes polyuria by glucosuria-mediated osmotic diuresis.
Metformin primarily reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and usually does not cause hypoglycemia alone.
Classic microvascular complications are retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy.

traps.wrong: HHS cannot occur because residual insulin normalizes glucose.
traps.right: Residual insulin may suppress ketones without controlling severe hyperglycemia.

traps.wrong: Serum potassium must be low in DKA.
traps.right: Serum potassium may be normal/high despite profound total-body depletion.

recognition: High glucose, ketones, and acidosis strongly suggest DKA.
Extreme hyperosmolarity with minimal ketones suggests HHS.
High insulin with low C-peptide points to injected insulin rather than beta-cell secretion.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Regulate body weight with long-term stores and short-term meals
lessons.subtitle: Leptin, adiponectin, ghrelin, hypothalamic circuits, and metabolic syndrome

visual.caption: Body weight reflects integration of adipose-store signals, meal signals, reward, and expenditure.

items.label: Long-term store
items.detail: Leptin rises with fat mass and normally suppresses appetite; common obesity usually has leptin resistance, not deficiency.

items.label: Insulin sensitivity
items.detail: Adiponectin supports fatty-acid oxidation and insulin action but falls as adiposity rises.

items.label: Meal timing
items.detail: Ghrelin rises before meals; gut satiety signals include CCK, PYY, and GLP-1.

items.label: Hypothalamus
items.detail: NPY/AgRP neurons promote feeding; POMC/CART melanocortin signaling suppresses it.

items.label: Visceral risk
items.detail: Visceral fat releases fatty acids and inflammatory mediators toward liver, promoting insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome.

essentials: BMI is kg/m2; adult obesity is conventionally BMI at least 30.
Visceral fat distribution predicts metabolic risk better than BMI alone.
Common obesity usually has elevated leptin with leptin resistance.
Metabolic syndrome combines central obesity, high triglycerides, low HDL, hypertension, and impaired glucose regulation.
Weight loss lowers leptin and energy expenditure, promoting hunger and regain.

traps.wrong: Most obesity is caused by congenital absence of leptin.
traps.right: Congenital leptin deficiency is rare; resistance to abundant leptin is common.

traps.wrong: Adiponectin rises with obesity.
traps.right: Adiponectin generally falls and insulin sensitivity worsens.

recognition: Orange-sized central adiposity with hypertension and high triglycerides suggests metabolic syndrome.
Ghrelin is the premeal hunger signal.
Rapid glycemic improvement after bariatric surgery reflects gut and hepatic signaling as well as later weight loss.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Convert nutrition numbers into clinical predictions
lessons.subtitle: DRIs, energy density, macronutrient ranges, fat quality, nitrogen balance, and malnutrition

visual.caption: First classify the reference value or nutrient, then predict the physiologic consequence.

items.label: Reference values
items.detail: EAR covers about half; RDA covers nearly all; AI substitutes when evidence is insufficient; UL marks the upper safety boundary.

items.label: Energy
items.detail: Carbohydrate 4 kcal/g, protein 4, fat 9, alcohol 7. Resting expenditure is usually the largest daily component.

items.label: AMDR
items.detail: Adults: carbohydrate 45-65%, fat 20-35%, protein 10-35% of energy.

items.label: Fat quality
items.detail: Trans fat raises LDL and may lower HDL; linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids are essential.

items.label: Protein-energy malnutrition
items.detail: Kwashiorkor causes edema and fatty liver; marasmus causes severe wasting without prominent edema.

essentials: Positive nitrogen balance occurs in growth, pregnancy, and recovery; trauma and starvation produce negative balance.
The limiting amino acid is the essential amino acid present in the lowest amount relative to need.
Soluble fiber can reduce cholesterol absorption and slow postprandial glucose rise.
Glycemic load accounts for both glycemic index and carbohydrate quantity.
Protein has the highest thermic effect of the major macronutrients.

traps.wrong: The UL is the ideal daily intake target.
traps.right: The UL is the highest chronic intake unlikely to cause harm.

traps.wrong: Kwashiorkor and marasmus both characteristically cause the same edema.
traps.right: Edema and fatty liver favor kwashiorkor; severe nonedematous wasting favors marasmus.

recognition: Low albumin with edema and fatty liver indicates kwashiorkor.
Severe loss of fat and muscle without edema indicates marasmus.
A serving-size question requires glycemic load rather than glycemic index alone.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Choose the molecular tool by what must be detected
lessons.subtitle: Restriction, cloning, PCR, probes, blots, sequencing, and expression analysis

visual.caption: The target molecule and the question being asked determine the correct technique.

items.label: Cut and clone
items.detail: Restriction enzymes cut specific often-palindromic sites; compatible ends align insert and vector and ligase seals them.

items.label: Amplify
items.detail: PCR repeats denaturation, primer annealing, and thermostable-polymerase extension.

items.label: Start from RNA
items.detail: Reverse transcriptase makes intron-free cDNA from mature mRNA before PCR or bacterial expression.

items.label: Blot
items.detail: Southern detects DNA, Northern RNA, and Western protein.

items.label: Read variation
items.detail: RFLP detects altered restriction fragments; Sanger ddNTPs terminate chains; microarrays compare many transcripts.

essentials: PCR primers define both boundaries and orientation of the amplicon.
Taq is thermostable but ordinary Taq has limited proofreading.
A cloning vector needs an origin, selectable marker, and insertion site.
Nucleic-acid probes depend on complementary hybridization and controlled stringency.
Dideoxynucleotides terminate extension because they lack a 3-prime hydroxyl.

traps.wrong: Western blot detects DNA.
traps.right: Western detects protein; Southern detects DNA and Northern detects RNA.

traps.wrong: Bacterial expression should use genomic human DNA with introns.
traps.right: Bacteria generally require intron-free cDNA.

recognition: A known sequence that must be amplified points to PCR.
Transcript abundance points to Northern, RT-qPCR, or expression array.
A single-base change affecting a restriction site can be detected by RFLP.
